notes.meaning: God tore the northern tribes away from David's royal line as a judgment for Solomon's sins. The people chose Jeroboam as their king, but Jeroboam forced them away from worshiping the Lord and set up golden calves instead. This rebellion led the whole northern kingdom into persistent evil.

The people of Israel continued in all the sins that Jeroboam had introduced. Generation after generation refused to turn back to God or worship at His temple in Jerusalem. Their stubbornness showed that the nation had completely embraced idolatry.

God finally banished the northern kingdom from His presence and His land, exactly as His prophets had warned for centuries. The Assyrian army conquered them and carried the people off into distant exile. Because they rejected the Lord, they lost their homeland and their national freedom.

The king of Assyria moved groups of foreigners from Babylonian and Syrian cities into Samaria to replace the exiled Israelites. These new settlers took over the towns and homes of the northern kingdom. This resettled population laid the foundation for the mixed people later known as the Samaritans.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient royal inscriptions show that King Sargon II of Assyria took credit for deporting Samaria's population and settling captive peoples from Babylon and Arabia in their place.

notes.meaning: When the new settlers first arrived in Samaria, they did not worship the Lord at all. God sent wild lions among them that attacked and killed some of the people. This judgment showed the pagan settlers that the God of Israel is the true ruler of the land.

The settlers sent word to the king of Assyria that lions were killing their people because they did not know the laws of the local deity. Like most pagans, they mistakenly thought the God of Israel was merely a regional god who had to be appeased with specific rituals. They wanted to learn the proper rites only to stop the attacks.

The Assyrian king commanded that one of the captive Israelite priests be sent back to Samaria to live there and teach the people. The king was not seeking the truth, but only wanted to protect his tax-paying subjects from the lions. People often seek religious remedies only when trouble strikes.

One of the exiled priests returned and settled in Bethel, where he instructed the people on how to fear the Lord. Because he was an Israelite priest from Bethel, he taught the corrupt calf-worship of Jeroboam rather than pure devotion to God. His lessons produced an outward ceremony rather than genuine faith.

Even with this instruction, each national group continued making its own idols. They placed these false gods in the hill shrines that the Israelites had previously built across the land. Instead of worshiping the Lord alone, they simply added Him to their list of deities.

The writer lists the various idols made by the settlers from Babylon, Cuth, Hamath, and Avva. The people of Sepharvaim engaged in the most terrible pagan practice by burning their own children in the fire to their false gods. These cruel rites demonstrated the complete spiritual darkness of the nations brought into the land.

The settlers showed outward respect to the Lord to avoid the lions, but they appointed common people from every class to act as priests at the high places. They ignored God's law, which limited the priesthood to the family of Aaron. Their worship was a human imitation rather than true obedience.

The new inhabitants feared the Lord out of dread, yet they continued to serve their own tribal gods according to their original customs. They attempted to blend the worship of the living God with heathen idolatry. God does not accept divided loyalty.

The writer observes that the settlers continued in these mixed practices down to his own day. Though they claimed to fear God, they did not truly fear Him because they ignored the laws He had given to Jacob's descendants. Trying to worship the true God alongside false idols means not truly worshiping Him at all.

The Lord had established a covenant, a sacred binding agreement, with Israel that strictly forbade bow-worship, service, or sacrifices to any other god. Complete loyalty to the Lord alone was the foundation of that relationship. God will not share His glory with any idol.

God reminded His people that He was the one who delivered them from slavery in Egypt with great power. Because He alone had rescued them, He alone had the right to demand their worship, fear, and sacrifices. Remembering God's past deliverance strengthens our trust in Him.

God had given His people written laws and commandments so they would know exactly how to live. They were commanded to obey these words continually and never turn aside to false gods. True devotion is shown by ongoing obedience to God's written Word.

The Lord pleaded with His people never to forget the covenant He had made with them. Once again, He repeated the urgent command not to fear or serve any other gods. God repeats His warnings because human hearts easily drift into compromise.

God promised that if His people would worship Him faithfully, He would defend them from all their enemies. They had no need for pagan rituals or foreign idols to stay secure. Real protection comes from resting in the Lord's power.

Despite God's clear warnings and promises, the people stubbornly refused to listen. They clung to their old pagan customs rather than following God's truth. A hardened heart will cling to sin even when God offers life and safety.

The chapter closes by summarizing the tragic compromise of these nations, who claimed to fear the Lord while bowing down to their idols. This mixed religion was passed down to their children and grandchildren for generations. A parent's spiritual compromise often becomes an enduring snare for future generations.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Historical studies observe that although the Samaritans began with this mixed idol-worship, they eventually abandoned all idols, adopted the five books of Moses, and became strictly monotheistic by the fourth century BC.
